title: Queues and Deques
summary: First in, first out for fair ordering and breadth-first search; two-ended access for window extremes.
keyPoints: A queue adds at the back and removes from the front, so the earliest item is handled first.
Breadth-first search uses a queue to visit nodes in order of distance.
A deque supports push and pop at both ends in O(1).
A monotonic deque keeps window maxima or minima without rescanning.

complexity.operation: Push or pop either end of a deque
complexity.note: All four operations are constant time.

commonMistakes: Using array shift on a large list in a loop; many languages implement it as an O(n) copy.
Using a stack for breadth-first search, which turns the traversal into depth-first order.
Forgetting to mark a node as visited when it is enqueued, so it is added many times.
Popping from a monotonic deque without checking whether the front is still inside the window.
interviewNotes: For BFS, say what the queue contains: all nodes at the same distance, waiting to expand.
If you need level-by-level processing, record the queue size before the inner loop.
For a window extreme, mention that a deque gives O(1) updates at both ends.

checkYourself.question: Why does BFS find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
checkYourself.answer: The queue visits every node at distance d before any node at distance d + 1, so the first time a node is reached is through a shortest path.

checkYourself.question: When is a deque better than a queue?
checkYourself.answer: When you need to add or remove at both ends, such as evicting an expired window maximum from the front while removing smaller candidates from the back.

checkYourself.question: How do you process a tree level by level?
checkYourself.answer: Before each level, record the current queue length. Process exactly that many nodes, adding their children to the back for the next level.
